# Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion
## Introduction
The **Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion** is a historic religious edifice located on Governors Island in New York Harbor. Ecclesiastically, it functions as a chapel of Trinity Church Wall Street, a prominent Episcopal parish in the Diocese of New York . Dedicated to St. Cornelius, the Roman centurion who is traditionally recognized as the first Gentile convert to Christianity, the chapel has served for nearly a century and a half as the primary spiritual home for the military personnel stationed at the Fort Columbus (later Fort Jay) garrison . The current structure, a limestone edifice designed by the noted architect Charles Coolidge Haight in the English Gothic style, was dedicated in 1906 and stands as a testament to the unique and enduring relationship between the Episcopal Church and the United States military .

The chapel is historically significant not only for its architecture but for its unusual administrative status. For much of its history, it operated under a specialized concordat between the Corporation of Trinity Church and the United States War Department . This agreement allowed a private religious entity to maintain a church and appoint clergy on federal military property, a situation described by historians as "unique among army posts" . Although regular religious services ceased following the departure of the United States Coast Guard in 1996, the building remains under the ownership of Trinity Church and has found new utility in the 21st century as a venue for public art and cultural interpretation .

## Historical Context and Foundation
### The Strategic and Social Environment of Governors Island
To fully appreciate the genesis of the Chapel of St. Cornelius, one must understand the environment of Governors Island in the mid-19th century. Known to the indigenous Lenape people as *Pagganck* and to the Dutch settlers as *Noten Eylandt* (Nut Island), the island occupies a strategic position in New York Harbor, approximately one half-mile from the southern tip of Manhattan . By the 18th century, it had been dedicated exclusively to military use, serving as a key component of the coastal defense system protecting New York City.

By the 1840s, the island housed the garrison of Fort Columbus and served as the principal recruiting depot for the United States Army . This function meant that a constant stream of soldiers—recruits, veterans, and officers—passed through the post. It was a transient and often harsh environment. Despite the large concentration of personnel and the social expectations of the era, which viewed religious observance as a cornerstone of moral discipline, the post lacked any dedicated religious infrastructure. Prior to the chapel's construction, divine services were conducted in ad-hoc settings: under groves of trees near "Colonel's Row" when the weather permitted, or within administrative rooms in the Post Headquarters when the climate was inclement . This lack of a sanctuary was a significant deficiency for a major federal installation.

### The Chaplaincy of the Rev. John McVickar (1844–1847)
The catalyst for the establishment of a permanent chapel was the Reverend John McVickar, S.T.D. (1787–1868). Appointed to the chaplaincy of Fort Columbus in 1844, McVickar was a figure of considerable standing in New York society and the Episcopal Church . A resident of New York City, he served simultaneously as the Professor of Moral and Intellectual Philosophy, Belles-Lettres, and Political Economy at Columbia College . His dual role as an academic and a military chaplain brought a level of intellectual rigor and social influence to the post that was previously absent.

Upon assuming his duties, McVickar was appalled by the lack of facilities for worship. He found "no place on the Island reserved for religious worship" and was forced to compete with military bureaucracy for space . McVickar, a man described as having "culture and distinction," was not content with the status quo. He possessed a "considerable initiative" and immediately began a campaign to rectify the situation .

### Conflict and Compromise with the War Department
McVickar’s initial proposal to build a chapel was met with resistance from the War Department in Washington. The federal government, at that time, did not have a standardized policy for constructing religious buildings on military posts. The Department’s response to McVickar’s request was bureaucratic and dismissive: it announced that it was "not accustomed to build chapels," had no appropriation for such a project, and, crucially, would not permit private entities to erect permanent structures on government land .

Undeterred, McVickar leveraged his personal connections. He was a close friend of General Winfield Scott, the Commanding General of the United States Army . McVickar traveled to Washington to appeal directly to Scott, bypassing the lower levels of the War Department bureaucracy. The result of this personal intervention was a compromise that allowed the project to proceed. The government agreed to lease a plot of land—approximately 150 feet square on the south side of the island—for the construction of a chapel . However, the lease contained a stipulation reflecting the island's primary martial purpose: the arrangement was "subject to the exigencies of war," meaning the government could reclaim the land if military necessity required it .

### Construction and Consecration of the First Chapel (1846–1847)
With the land secured, McVickar undertook the responsibility of funding and designing the structure himself. He solicited private subscriptions, securing a "generous contribution" from the Corporation of Trinity Church, the wealthy and influential parish in lower Manhattan . McVickar also drafted the architectural plans for the building.

The first Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion was completed in 1846 . It was a wooden structure, described in contemporary accounts as a "neat and tasteful church-like building" . The choice of dedication was highly symbolic. Cornelius the Centurion, described in the tenth chapter of the Acts of the Apostles, was a Roman officer stationed in Caesarea who feared God and gave alms generously. He is revered as the first Gentile convert to Christianity . By dedicating the chapel to St. Cornelius, McVickar provided the soldiers of Governors Island with a patron saint who embodied the compatibility of military service and Christian piety—a "just man" who served an earthly empire while acknowledging a heavenly one .

The chapel was formally consecrated on April 19, 1847 . For the next twenty years, it served as the center of religious life on the island, hosting services for soldiers departing for the Mexican-American War and the Civil War .

## The Concordat of 1868: A Unique Church-State Partnership
### The Post-Civil War Crisis (1866)
The relationship between the chapel and the military authorities underwent a profound transformation in the years following the American Civil War. In 1866, as part of a broader reorganization and retrenchment of the armed forces, the War Department ceased providing commissioned chaplains to Governors Island . The official rationale for this decision was geographical: because Governors Island was situated within the municipal limits of New York City, the Department argued that the "religious denominations of that city ought to feel interest enough in the spiritual welfare of the men on the Island to supply them with the ministrations of religion" .

This decision effectively privatized the spiritual care of the garrison, threatening to leave the post without a resident clergyman. The burden of filling this void fell upon the local religious community. Trinity Church, which had already supported the construction of the chapel and had a long history of missionary work, viewed this withdrawal of state support as an opportunity to formalize its presence on the island .

### The Agreement of 1868
In response to the War Department's action, the Rector and Vestry of Trinity Church opened negotiations with the federal government. They proposed a "Concordat" or agreement that would ensure the continuity of worship at St. Cornelius. Trinity offered to maintain a chaplain at its own expense—paying his salary and covering the operational costs of the chapel—if the Army would agree to place the chapel under the parish's control and grant the civilian priest the privileges of a military officer .

The War Department accepted this offer in August 1868 . The terms of the agreement were specific and established a hybrid status for the chapel:

1. **Ecclesiastical Status**: St. Cornelius became a "free chapel" of Trinity Parish, meaning it was administratively part of the parish but did not charge pew rents, which was a common practice at the time . 
2. **Status of the Chaplain**: The government agreed to provide the clergyman paid by Trinity with "quarters, fuel, and the facilities" typically accorded to commissioned officers . 
3. **Duties**: The Trinity-appointed priest was authorized to "officiate regularly on Governor's Island, to teach the Schools and perform all the duties imposed on Chaplains by the Army regulations" . 
4. **Property**: The use of the chapel building was formally ceded to the parish for religious purposes .

This arrangement was described by the Episcopal journalist and historian Clifford Phelps Morehouse as "unique among army posts" . It effectively created a private ecclesiastical enclave within a federal military installation, blurring the lines between church and state in a manner that was pragmatic for the time.

### Evolution of the Agreement (1924–1966)
This partnership endured for nearly a century, though it was modified periodically to reflect changing circumstances.

* **1924 Modification**: Following the retirement of the Reverend Edmund Banks Smith, a long-serving vicar who oversaw the construction of the new chapel, the agreement was renegotiated. The Army resumed the responsibility of paying the chaplain's salary. However, to maintain the link with Trinity, the military chaplain assigned to the post—who was required to be an Episcopal priest—was simultaneously appointed as an "honorary vicar" of Trinity Church . Trinity continued to maintain the physical fabric of the building. 
* **1954 Modification**: Reflecting the increasing religious diversity of the military and the ecumenical movement, the agreement was adjusted to allow chaplains from other Protestant denominations to use St. Cornelius for services . 
* **1966 Transfer**: When control of Governors Island passed from the Army to the Coast Guard, the Navy Chaplain Corps assumed responsibility for assigning clergy. The specific denominational requirement was relaxed, but the historical connection to Trinity remained through the ownership of the building .

## The Second Chapel: Architecture and Construction (1905–1906)
### Deterioration of the Wooden Chapel
By the beginning of the 20th century, the original 1847 wooden chapel had reached the end of its structural life. After "nearly sixty years of constant use," the building was in a state of "partial decay" . Reports from the era detailed significant deficiencies: the floor had rotted, the roof and siding leaked, and the structure was "very cold in winter" . In one instance, a window frame fell out of the wall during a high wind, underscoring the danger the building posed to the congregation .

Trinity Church faced a decision: repair the failing wooden structure or build anew. Despite the sentimental associations connected with the old chapel, the Corporation decided that restoration was impractical. They resolved to replace the wooden building with a permanent stone edifice that would reflect the dignity of the parish and the permanence of the military post .

### Negotiations and Approvals (1904–1905)
Constructing a major stone church on federal land required high-level approval. Negotiations with the War Department spanned the years 1904 and 1905 . The Vestry of Trinity Church worked closely with military officials, including Major General Frederick D. Grant (son of Ulysses S. Grant) and Secretary of War William Howard Taft, to secure permission for the new building . The Army designated a new site for the chapel, located slightly to the north and east of the original footprint .

### The Architect: Charles Coolidge Haight
For this prestigious commission, Trinity Church selected the architect Charles Coolidge Haight (1841–1917) . Haight was one of the most respected architects of his generation, known particularly for his work in the "Collegiate Gothic" style at Yale University and the General Theological Seminary in New York . His connection to the project was both professional and personal; he had served in the Civil War, giving him a unique appreciation for the martial context of the chapel .

Haight's design for St. Cornelius is considered a prime example of his "Parish Gothic" style—a mode of architecture that emphasized rugged masonry, restraint in ornamentation, and a focus on mass and proportion rather than delicate tracery .

### Architectural Description
The new Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion was dedicated on October 19, 1906, following the laying of the cornerstone on October 27, 1905 .

#### Exterior
The chapel is constructed of buff Indiana limestone, a material chosen for its durability and aesthetic warmth . The plan is cruciform, featuring a nave, transepts, and a deep chancel. The total length of the building is 106 feet, with a width of 70 feet across the transepts .

The most striking exterior feature is the massive, square tower rising from the crossing. This three-story tower serves as a landmark on the island, visible from the harbor and echoing the defensive architecture of the nearby fortifications . The roof is sheathed in slate, contributing to the English Gothic character . The cornerstone, inscribed "A.D. 1905," is located at the east end of the building .

#### Interior
The interior of the chapel is characterized by its solemnity and light. The walls are faced with the same limestone as the exterior, creating a unified and bright aesthetic .

* **Nave**: The nave is designed to accommodate the garrison congregation. Unlike many civilian churches of the era, it was furnished with movable chairs rather than fixed pews, allowing for flexibility in military ceremonies . 
* **Chancel**: The chancel is equipped with carved oak choir stalls and clergy seats, reflecting the Anglican emphasis on choral liturgy . 
* **Crypt**: Beneath the chancel lies a crypt and a mortuary chapel. The roof of this subterranean space is vaulted with flat Italian tile, a structural technique Haight often employed to ensure fireproofing and durability . 
* **Side Chapel**: A smaller side chapel, dedicated to St. Alban, provides a space for more intimate services .

### Table 1: Architectural Specifications
| Feature | Detail |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Architect** | Charles Coolidge Haight |
| **Style** | English Gothic / Gothic Revival |
| **Construction Dates** | 1905–1906 |
| **Primary Material** | Buff Indiana Limestone |
| **Roof Material** | Slate |
| **Length** | 106 feet |
| **Width (at Transepts)** | 70 feet |
| **Layout** | Cruciform (Nave, Transepts, Chancel, Side Chapel) |
| **Tower** | Three-story square tower at crossing |

## Art, Iconography, and Memorials
The Chapel of St. Cornelius was designed to function not only as a place of worship but also as a repository of military memory. Over the 20th century, it acquired a significant collection of stained glass, statuary, and battle flags that narrated the history of the American Army.

### The Reredos and Altar
The visual focus of the sanctuary is the high altar and its accompanying reredos (altar screen). The reredos features a triptych of painted panels or sculptures depicting "Three Military Saints," reinforcing the chapel's specific dedication .

1. **St. Cornelius**: Depicted on the right side, the patron of the chapel is shown in the garb of a Roman officer. 
2. **St. Martin of Tours**: In the center, St. Martin is depicted in the act of cutting his military cloak to share it with a beggar—a classic iconographic representation of charity and the transition from soldier to saint . 
3. **St. George**: On the left, St. George is shown in armor slaying the dragon, symbolizing courage and the triumph of good over evil .

These figures provided a theological anchor for the soldiers worshiping there, offering models of sanctity that were compatible with the profession of arms.

### Stained Glass Windows
The chapel contains approximately 35 stained glass windows, filling the limestone interior with colored light . The glazing program is a mix of biblical narratives and specific military memorials.

* **The Cornelius Window**: One of the most significant windows illustrates the biblical story of the chapel's patron. It is a two-part composition. The left section depicts Cornelius in Caesarea hearing the angel's command to send for Peter (Acts 10:1-5). The right section shows the meeting between Cornelius and Peter. Interestingly, the figure of Peter is not explicitly depicted in the meeting scene, focusing the viewer's attention entirely on Cornelius's act of devotion . 
* **The Hancock Memorial Window**: A prominent window is dedicated to the memory of Major General Winfield Scott Hancock. Hancock, a hero of the Battle of Gettysburg, commanded the Department of the East from Governors Island starting in 1878\. He was a major figure in the post's history, having run for President in 1880 and organized the funeral of Ulysses S. Grant from the island in 1885 . 
* **The Barry Window**: Located over the altar, this window honors Brevet Major General William F. Barry, the "Father of the Artillery School," who served as Commandant from 1867 to 1877 . It features jeweled glass and the inscription "I have fought the good fight" . 
* **The Easterbrook Windows**: Several windows honor the family of Chaplain (Colonel) Edmund P. Easterbrook, who served as Chief of Chaplains. One window, depicting the "Good Shepherd," was given by his five children, while another, depicting the "Blessed Mother and Child," honors his wife, Fannie Luscombe Easterbrook .

### The Battle Flag Collection
Perhaps the most distinctive feature of the chapel's interior was its extensive collection of battle flags. For much of the 20th century, the nave and chancel were hung with the tattered colors of regiments that had been stationed at Fort Jay, transforming the space into a military shrine .

By 2010, the collection numbered 87 flags . The oldest flag in the collection dated back to approximately 1787\. The collection included:

* **Mexican-American War Flags**: Banners carried by the 1st Regiment of New York Volunteers during the Mexican campaigns were displayed in the south transept . These flags saw action at the battles of Chapultepec and Veracruz. 
* **Civil War and Boxer Rebellion**: The collection included flags from the Civil War and a large American flag from the Boxer Rebellion in China . 
* **The King's Royal Rifle Corps Flag**: In 1921, the British Army donated a regimental color from the King's Royal Rifle Corps (originally the Royal American Regiment, raised on Governors Island in the 18th century) to the chapel. This gift was a gesture of goodwill and alliance between the United Kingdom and the United States following World War I .

The preservation of these fragile textiles was a constant concern. In the 1920s, Trinity Church funded a major restoration project to stabilize the flags, which were suffering from the effects of gravity and light .

### Organ
The chapel is equipped with a pipe organ located in a chamber on the south side of the chancel . The original instrument installed in the new chapel was built by the M.P. Möller company. This instrument served the congregation for decades but eventually required replacement. In the 1980s, the Möller organ was replaced by a Rodgers electronic organ (Model 926), a decision likely driven by the maintenance challenges of a pipe organ in a building exposed to the damp harbor environment .

## The Chapel in the 20th and 21st Centuries
### The World Wars and Cold War Era
Throughout the two World Wars, Governors Island was a hive of activity, serving as a headquarters and embarkation point for troops heading to Europe. The Chapel of St. Cornelius played a central role in the lives of these soldiers, hosting services of farewell and thanksgiving. The collection of memorial plaques on the walls grew during this period, recording the names of officers and men who departed from the island never to return .

In 1966, the U.S. Army transferred jurisdiction of Governors Island to the U.S. Coast Guard. The island became the Coast Guard's largest installation, serving as a self-contained community for approximately 3,500 personnel and their families . During this "Coast Guard Era," the chapel continued to function as an active parish. It was the site of countless baptisms, weddings, and funerals, binding the military community together. Although the specific agreement regarding the chaplaincy evolved, with Navy chaplains replacing Army ones, the building remained the property of Trinity Church .

In the early 1970s, Trinity Church discontinued its practice of providing ordinary maintenance and janitorial services, shifting these operational costs to the military. However, the parish continued to assist with major capital maintenance and provided insurance coverage, maintaining its stewardship of the historic fabric .

### Decommissioning and Reversion (1996)
The closure of the Coast Guard base in 1996 marked the end of the chapel's life as an active military place of worship. As the military departed, the legal agreements governing the chapel came into play. In 1986, Trinity had technically donated the chapel to the U.S. Government, but with a crucial stipulation: a reversionary clause stated that if the government ceased to own the land or use the building as a military chapel, ownership would revert to Trinity Church .

With the cessation of military operations, this clause was triggered. Trinity Church regained full control of the empty edifice. The battle flags and many relics remained within the silent sanctuary. When the rest of Governors Island was transferred to the people of New York in 2003 (administered by the Trust for Governors Island), the chapel remained a private inholding owned by Trinity .

### Contemporary Use and Cultural Revitalization
In the 21st century, the Chapel of St. Cornelius has been integrated into the cultural programming of the revitalized Governors Island. While it does not hold regular religious services, Trinity Church has allowed the space to be used for site-specific art installations and performances that engage with its architecture and history .

A notable example of this adaptive reuse was the 2018 installation *The Eclipse* by artist Jacob Hashimoto. This work featured thousands of suspended monochrome disks creating a "cloud" within the nave. The installation interacted with the light filtering through Haight's stained glass windows, creating a contemplative atmosphere that respected the building's sacred origins while offering a new experience for visitors . Such events have allowed the general public to access the interior of the chapel, which had been restricted to military personnel and their guests for most of its history.

## Significance and Legacy
### As a Model of Church-State Cooperation
The Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion stands as a rare example of a "free chapel" operating on federal land. The agreements of 1868 and 1924 created a model of cooperation between church and state that is virtually unknown in modern American jurisprudence . It allowed a private religious corporation to embed itself in the military command structure, providing a continuity of pastoral care and architectural maintenance that survived shifting political winds and budget cuts. This partnership ensured that the soldiers of Governors Island had access to a religious facility of a quality far surpassing standard military issue.

### Architectural Legacy
Architecturally, the chapel is a significant work in the oeuvre of Charles C. Haight. It demonstrates his ability to adapt the "Collegiate Gothic" vocabulary to a military context. The building's massing, use of materials, and integration with the landscape of the island make it a critical component of the Governors Island Historic District . It stands as a "spiritual anchor" on the island, a stone witness to the thousands of American soldiers who passed through its doors during the nation's most pivotal conflicts.

Under the 1868 agreement, the Trinity-appointed priest was authorized to "officiate regularly on Governor's Island, to teach the Schools and perform all the duties imposed on Chaplains by the Army regulations".
Under the 1868 agreement, the use of the chapel building was formally ceded to Trinity Parish for religious purposes.
The 1868 arrangement was described by the Episcopal journalist and historian Clifford Phelps Morehouse as "unique among army posts".

The 1868 arrangement effectively created a private ecclesiastical enclave within a federal military installation, blurring the lines between church and state in a manner that was pragmatic for the time.
The partnership between the Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion and the military endured for nearly a century, though it was modified periodically to reflect changing circumstances.
Following the retirement of the Reverend Edmund Banks Smith, a long-serving vicar who oversaw the construction of the new chapel, the agreement was renegotiated in 1924.
In the 1924 modification, the Army resumed the responsibility of paying the chaplain's salary.

To maintain the link with Trinity Church, the military chaplain assigned to the post, who was required to be an Episcopal priest, was simultaneously appointed as an "honorary vicar" of Trinity Church.
Trinity Church continued to maintain the physical fabric of the Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion building.

In 1954, reflecting the increasing religious diversity of the military and the ecumenical movement, the agreement was adjusted to allow chaplains from other Protestant denominations to use St. Cornelius for services.
In 1966, control of Governors Island passed from the Army to the Coast Guard.
The Navy Chaplain Corps assumed responsibility for assigning clergy when control of Governors Island passed to the Coast Guard.
The specific denominational requirement for chaplains was relaxed, but the historical connection to Trinity Church remained through the ownership of the building.
By the beginning of the 20th century, the original 1847 wooden chapel had reached the end of its structural life.
After "nearly sixty years of constant use," the original 1847 wooden chapel building was in a state of "partial decay".
Reports from the era detailed significant deficiencies in the original wooden chapel: the floor had rotted, the roof and siding leaked, and the structure was "very cold in winter".
In one instance, a window frame fell out of the wall of the original wooden chapel during a high wind, underscoring the danger the building posed to the congregation.
Trinity Church faced a decision: repair the failing wooden structure or build anew.
Despite the sentimental associations connected with the old chapel, the Corporation of Trinity Church decided that restoration was impractical.
Trinity Church resolved to replace the wooden building with a permanent stone edifice that would reflect the dignity of the parish and the permanence of the military post.
Constructing a major stone church on federal land required high-level approval.
Negotiations with the War Department for the new chapel spanned the years 1904 and 1905.
The Vestry of Trinity Church worked closely with military officials, including Major General Frederick D. Grant and Secretary of War William Howard Taft, to secure permission for the new building.
The Army designated a new site for the chapel, located slightly to the north and east of the original footprint.
For this prestigious commission, Trinity Church selected the architect Charles Coolidge Haight (1841–1917).

Charles Coolidge Haight was one of the most respected architects of his generation, known particularly for his work in the "Collegiate Gothic" style at Yale University and the General Theological Seminary in New York.
Charles Coolidge Haight's connection to the project was both professional and personal.
Charles Coolidge Haight had served in the Civil War, giving him a unique appreciation for the martial context of the chapel.
Charles Coolidge Haight's design for St. Cornelius is considered a prime example of his "Parish Gothic" style.
Charles Coolidge Haight's "Parish Gothic" style emphasized rugged masonry, restraint in ornamentation, and a focus on mass and proportion rather than delicate tracery.
The new Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion was dedicated on October 19, 1906, following the laying of the cornerstone on October 27, 1905.
The chapel is constructed of buff Indiana limestone, a material chosen for its durability and aesthetic warmth.
The chapel's plan is cruciform, featuring a nave, transepts, and a deep chancel.
The total length of the chapel building is 106 feet.
The width of the chapel building across the transepts is 70 feet.
The most striking exterior feature of the chapel is the massive, square tower rising from the crossing.
This three-story tower serves as a landmark on Governors Island, visible from the harbor and echoing the defensive architecture of the nearby fortifications.
The roof of the chapel is sheathed in slate, contributing to the English Gothic character.
The cornerstone of the chapel, inscribed "A.D. 1905," is located at the east end of the building.
The interior of the chapel is characterized by its solemnity and light.
The walls of the chapel's interior are faced with the same limestone as the exterior, creating a unified and bright aesthetic.
The nave of the chapel is designed to accommodate the garrison congregation.

Unlike many civilian churches of the era, the nave of the Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion was furnished with movable chairs rather than fixed pews, allowing for flexibility in military ceremonies.
The chancel of the chapel is equipped with carved oak choir stalls and clergy seats, reflecting the Anglican emphasis on choral liturgy.
Beneath the chancel lies a crypt and a mortuary chapel.
The roof of the subterranean space (crypt and mortuary chapel) is vaulted with flat Italian tile, a structural technique Charles Coolidge Haight often employed to ensure fireproofing and durability.
A smaller side chapel, dedicated to St. Alban, provides a space for more intimate services.
The Chapel of St. Cornelius was designed to function not only as a place of worship but also as a repository of military memory.
Over the 20th century, the Chapel of St. Cornelius acquired a significant collection of stained glass, statuary, and battle flags that narrated the history of the American Army.
The visual focus of the sanctuary is the high altar and its accompanying reredos (altar screen).
The reredos features a triptych of painted panels or sculptures depicting "Three Military Saints," reinforcing the chapel's specific dedication.
St. Cornelius is depicted on the right side of the reredos in the garb of a Roman officer.
In the center of the reredos, St. Martin of Tours is depicted in the act of cutting his military cloak to share it with a beggar.
St. Martin of Tours' depiction is a classic iconographic representation of charity and the transition from soldier to saint.
On the left of the reredos, St. George is shown in armor slaying the dragon, symbolizing courage and the triumph of good over evil.
These figures provided a theological anchor for the soldiers worshiping there, offering models of sanctity that were compatible with the profession of arms.
The chapel contains approximately 35 stained glass windows, filling the limestone interior with colored light.
The glazing program of the chapel is a mix of biblical narratives and specific military memorials.
One of the most significant windows, the Cornelius Window, illustrates the biblical story of the chapel's patron.
The Cornelius Window is a two-part composition.
The left section of the Cornelius Window depicts Cornelius in Caesarea hearing the angel's command to send for Peter (Acts 10:1-5).
The right section of the Cornelius Window shows the meeting between Cornelius and Peter.
The figure of Peter is not explicitly depicted in the meeting scene of the Cornelius Window, focusing the viewer's attention entirely on Cornelius's act of devotion.
A prominent window is dedicated to the memory of Major General Winfield Scott Hancock.
Major General Winfield Scott Hancock was a hero of the Battle of Gettysburg.
Major General Winfield Scott Hancock commanded the Department of the East from Governors Island starting in 1878.
Major General Winfield Scott Hancock was a major figure in Governors Island's history.
Major General Winfield Scott Hancock ran for President in 1880.
Major General Winfield Scott Hancock organized the funeral of Ulysses S. Grant from Governors Island in 1885.
The Barry Window, located over the altar, honors Brevet Major General William F. Barry, the "Father of the Artillery School".
Brevet Major General William F. Barry served as Commandant from 1867 to 1877.
The Barry Window features jeweled glass and the inscription "I have fought the good fight".
Several windows honor the family of Chaplain (Colonel) Edmund P. Easterbrook, who served as Chief of Chaplains.
One window, depicting the "Good Shepherd," was given by Chaplain (Colonel) Edmund P. Easterbrook's five children.
Another window, depicting the "Blessed Mother and Child," honors Chaplain (Colonel) Edmund P. Easterbrook's wife, Fannie Luscombe Easterbrook.
Perhaps the most distinctive feature of the chapel's interior was its extensive collection of battle flags.

For much of the 20th century, the nave and chancel of the Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion were hung with the tattered colors of regiments that had been stationed at Fort Jay, transforming the space into a military shrine.
By 2010, the battle flag collection numbered 87 flags.
The oldest flag in the collection dated back to approximately 1787.
The collection included Mexican-American War Flags.
Banners carried by the 1st Regiment of New York Volunteers during the Mexican campaigns were displayed in the south transept.
These flags saw action at the battles of Chapultepec and Veracruz.
The collection included flags from the Civil War and a large American flag from the Boxer Rebellion in China.
In 1921, the British Army donated a regimental color from the King's Royal Rifle Corps (originally the Royal American Regiment, raised on Governors Island in the 18th century) to the chapel.
This gift was a gesture of goodwill and alliance between the United Kingdom and the United States following World War I.
The preservation of these fragile textiles was a constant concern.
In the 1920s, Trinity Church funded a major restoration project to stabilize the flags, which were suffering from the effects of gravity and light.
The chapel is equipped with a pipe organ located in a chamber on the south side of the chancel.
The original instrument installed in the new chapel was built by the M.P. Möller company.
This instrument served the congregation for decades but eventually required replacement.
In the 1980s, the Möller organ was replaced by a Rodgers electronic organ (Model 926).
The decision to replace the Möller organ was likely driven by the maintenance challenges of a pipe organ in a building exposed to the damp harbor environment.
Throughout the two World Wars, Governors Island was a hive of activity, serving as a headquarters and embarkation point for troops heading to Europe.
The Chapel of St. Cornelius played a central role in the lives of these soldiers, hosting services of farewell and thanksgiving.
The collection of memorial plaques on the walls grew during this period, recording the names of officers and men who departed from the island never to return.
In 1966, the U.S. Army transferred jurisdiction of Governors Island to the U.S. Coast Guard.
Governors Island became the Coast Guard's largest installation, serving as a self-contained community for approximately 3,500 personnel and their families.
During this "Coast Guard Era," the chapel continued to function as an active parish.
The Chapel of St. Cornelius was the site of countless baptisms, weddings, and funerals, binding the military community together.
Although the specific agreement regarding the chaplaincy evolved, with Navy chaplains replacing Army ones, the building remained the property of Trinity Church.
In the early 1970s, Trinity Church discontinued its practice of providing ordinary maintenance and janitorial services, shifting these operational costs to the military.
Trinity Church continued to assist with major capital maintenance and provided insurance coverage, maintaining its stewardship of the historic fabric.
The closure of the Coast Guard base in 1996 marked the end of the chapel's life as an active military place of worship.
As the military departed, the legal agreements governing the chapel came into play.
In 1986, Trinity had technically donated the chapel to the U.S. Government, but with a crucial stipulation.
A reversionary clause stated that if the government ceased to own the land or use the building as a military chapel, ownership would revert to Trinity Church.
With the cessation of military operations, this clause was triggered.
Trinity Church regained full control of the empty edifice.
The battle flags and many relics remained within the silent sanctuary.
When the rest of Governors Island was transferred to the people of New York in 2003 (administered by the Trust for Governors Island), the chapel remained a private inholding owned by Trinity.
In the 21st century, the Chapel of St. Cornelius has been integrated into the cultural programming of the revitalized Governors Island.
While it does not hold regular religious services, Trinity Church has allowed the space to be used for site-specific art installations and performances that engage with its architecture and history.
A notable example of this adaptive reuse was the 2018 installation *The Eclipse* by artist Jacob Hashimoto.
This work featured thousands of suspended monochrome disks creating a "cloud" within the nave.

The installation interacted with the light filtering through Haight's stained glass windows, creating a contemplative atmosphere that respected the building's sacred origins while offering a new experience for visitors.
Such events have allowed the general public to access the interior of the chapel, which had been restricted to military personnel and their guests for most of its history.
The Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion stands as a rare example of a "free chapel" operating on federal land.
The agreements of 1868 and 1924 created a model of cooperation between church and state that is virtually unknown in modern American jurisprudence.

It allowed a private religious corporation to embed itself in the military command structure, providing a continuity of pastoral care and architectural maintenance that survived shifting political winds and budget cuts.
This partnership ensured that the soldiers of Governors Island had access to a religious facility of a quality far surpassing standard military issue.
Architecturally, the chapel is a significant work in the oeuvre of Charles C. Haight.
The Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion demonstrates Charles C. Haight's ability to adapt the "Collegiate Gothic" vocabulary to a military context.
The building's massing, use of materials, and integration with the landscape of Governors Island make it a critical component of the Governors Island Historic District.

The Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion stands as a "spiritual anchor" on Governors Island, a stone witness to the thousands of American soldiers who passed through its doors during the nation's most pivotal conflicts.

4.title: St. Cornelius Chapel - Governors Island, New York City
4.content: ![Image 1: 1910 Postcard of the Episcopal Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion - Governors Island, New York City](https://www.nycago.org/Organs/NYC/img/StCorneliusEpis1910PC.jpg) Click on images to enlarge Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion **(Episcopal)** Governors Island New York Harbor New York, N.Y. 10004 **Organ Specifications:** Present Chapel (since 1905) • Rodgers Instruments electronic (1990s) ► [II/6 M.P. Möller, Inc., Op. 8673](https://www.nycago.org/Organs/NYC/html/StCorneliusCenturion.html#Moller) (1954) • II/18 Hook & Hastings, Op. 2115 (1906) Original Chapel (1847-1905) • unknown, if any ![Image 2: Aerial View of Governors Island, New York City](https://www.nycago.org/Organs/NYC/img/GovernorsIsAerial.jpg) Governors Island is located in the New York Harbor, approximately one-half mile from Battery Park in Lower Manhattan and one-quarter mile from Brooklyn. Its waterfront offers some of the most dramatic and impressive vistas of the New York skyline and New York Harbor, including the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island. Physically, the Island changed greatly during the early twentieth century. Using rocks and dirt from the excavations for the Lexington Avenue Subway, the Army Corps of Engineers supervised the deposit of 4,787,000 cubic yards of fill on the south side of Governors Island, adding 103 acres of flat, treeless land by 1912, and bringing the total acreage of the Island to 172. The island has nearly 225 buildings, considerable open space, and recreational amenities. The northern half of the Island, consisting of approximately 92 acres, has been designated as both a National Historic Landmark District and a New York City Historic District, and features late 18th and early 19th century fortifications, pre-Civil War arsenal buildings, Victorian and Romanesque Revival housing, as well as early 20th century neo-classical architecture. Five buildings within the Historic District, including Fort Jay and Castle Williams, are individually listed in the National Register of Historic Places. The Native Americans of the Manhattan region referred to the island as Pagganck (“Nut Island”) after the Island’s plentiful hickory, oak and chestnut trees. In June of 1637, Wouter Van Twiller, representative of Holland, purchased the island from the Native Americans of Manahatas for two ax heads, a string of beads, and a handful of nails. The Island, thereafter known as Noten Eylant or Nutten Island, was confiscated by the Dutch Government a year later. In 1664 the English captured New Amsterdam, renaming it New York, and took Nutten Island, which had been left unfortified by the Dutch. The island, however, switched hands between the British and the Dutch over the next 10 years until the British regained exclusive control of the island for the “benefit and accommodation of His Majesty's Governors.” Although it was not officially named until 1784, it thus came to be called Governors Island. The island’s strategic location resulted in its use as a military facility by British and American forces for over 200 years. In 1794, with the country in need of a system of coastal defenses, construction began on Fort Jay, on high ground in the center of the Island. In 1800, New York transferred the Island to the United States government for military purposes. During the American Civil War, it was used for recruitment and as a prison for captured Confederate soldiers. Throughout World Wars I and II, the Island served as an important supply base for Army ground and air forces. With the consolidation of U.S. Military forces in 1966, the island was transferred to the Coast Guard, making it their largest installation. Governors Island served as a self-contained residential community, with an on-island population of approximately 3,500, and as a base of operations for the Atlantic Area Command and Maintenance and Logistics Command as well as the Captain of the Port of New York. In 1995, the Coast Guard closed its facilities on Governors Island and all residential personnel were relocated. President Clinton designated 22 acres of the island, including the two great forts, as the Governors Island National Monument in January 2001, and on April 1, 2002, it was announced that the United States of America would sell Governors Island to the people of New York for a nominal cost. On January 31, 2003, the island was transferred to the people of New York through the Governors Island Preservation and Education Corporation. ![Image 3: Original Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion - Governors Island, New York City](https://www.nycago.org/Organs/NYC/img/StCorneliusOldChapelExt3.jpg) Original chapel The original chapel on Governors Island dates back to 1846 when the Rev. John McVickar, D.D., was appointed chaplain for the Army servicemen and their families on the island. Services were held under the trees in fair weather, and in the post headquarters at other times. Dr. McVickar soon campaigned for an adequate post chapel, but the Government was not accustomed to building chapels, nor was it willing to make an appropriation for the purpose. Dr. McVickar counted among his friends the Commander-in-Chief of the Army, General Scott, and shortly the Government agreed to lease about 150 feet square on the south side of the island as a site for a chapel, subject to the exigencies of war. The chaplain set about raising private subscriptions for a chapel, and received a generous contribution from the corporation of Trinity Church, New York. In 1847, "a neat and tasteful church-like building of wood" was constructed after the chaplain's own plans from funds collected by himself. Thereafter, from 1846 to 1855, Trinity Church made an annual appropriation for its support, and in 1868, the chapel became part of Trinity Parish. ![Image 4: Original Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion - Governors Island, New York City](https://www.nycago.org/Organs/NYC/img/StCorneliusOldChapelExt.jpg) Original chapel with new chapel at rear By the beginning of the 20th century, the 1847 chapel was in such disrepair that Trinity deemed it unsalvageable. In 1905, the Army accepted Trinity's offer to build a new chapel, and in October, 1905, the cornerstone was laid for the present building. Just a year later, on October 19, 1906, the new chapel with the old name, the Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion, was dedicated by Bishop David Greer, assisted by the clergy of Trinity Parish, New York. The music for the occasion was furnished by the choir of Trinity Church, under the direction of Mr. Victor Baier, and by the choir of the post chapel, under the direction of Lt. A. F. Halpin (retired), the post organist. ![Image 5: Episcopal Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion - Governors Island, New York City](https://www.nycago.org/Organs/NYC/img/StCorneliusInt1.jpg) The new chapel was designed by Charles C. Haight in the English Gothic style of the 14th century. It is a cruciform structure of buff Indiana limestone with a massive tower, nave, transepts, chancel, and side chapel. The total length is 106 feet and the greatest width 70 feet. Carved oak clergy and choir seats are provided, while the nave and St. Albans Chapel have chairs. The clergy and choir sacristies and the organ are on the south side of the chancel. Under the chancel is a mortuary chapel, and the roof of this and the entire crypt is vaulted with flat Italian tile. Until recently the chapel housed historically significant battle flags and other symbolic relics. Governors Island has two other chapels: Our Lady, Star of the Sea (Roman Catholic, built in 1942) and a Jewish Chapel.

**Cornelius** ([Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): Κορνήλιος, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Greek "Romanization of Greek"):_Kornḗlios_; [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): _Cornēlius_[[kɔrˈneː.li.ʊs]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Latin "Help:IPA/Latin"); fl. 1st century AD) was a [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire")[centurion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centurion "Centurion") who is considered by some [Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians") to be the first [Gentile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentile "Gentile") to [convert to the faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_to_Christianity "Conversion to Christianity"), as related in [Acts of the Apostles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_the_Apostles "Acts of the Apostles") (see [Ethiopian eunuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_eunuch "Ethiopian eunuch") for the competing tradition). The baptism of Cornelius is an important event in the history of the early Christian church. He may have belonged to the [gens Cornelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gens_Cornelia "Gens Cornelia"), a prominent Roman family.

Biblical account
----------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cornelius_the_Centurion&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biblical account")]

Cornelius was a centurion in the [Cohors II Italica Civium Romanorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohors_II_Italica_Civium_Romanorum "Cohors II Italica Civium Romanorum"), mentioned as _Cohors Italica_ in the [Vulgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate "Vulgate").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-4) He was stationed in [Caesarea Maritima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesarea_Maritima "Caesarea Maritima"), the capital of Roman [Iudaea province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaea_(Roman_province) "Judaea (Roman province)").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-cathen-5) He is depicted in the [New Testament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Testament "New Testament") as a [God-fearing man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God-fearer "God-fearer")[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-6) who always prayed and was full of good works and deeds of [alms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alms "Alms"). Cornelius receives a vision in which an [angel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel "Angel") of God tells him that his prayers have been heard; he understands that he has been chosen for a higher alternative. The angel then instructs Cornelius to send the men of his household to [Joppa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaffa "Jaffa"), where they will find [Simon Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Peter "Saint Peter"), who is residing with a [tanner by the name of Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_the_Tanner_(New_Testament) "Simon the Tanner (New Testament)") ([Acts 10:5ff](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bible_(King_James)/Acts#10:5 "s:Bible (King James)/Acts")).

The [conversion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conversion_to_Christianity "Conversion to Christianity") of Cornelius comes after [a separate vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter%27s_vision_of_a_sheet_with_animals "Peter's vision of a sheet with animals") given to Simon Peter ([Acts 10:10–16](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bible_(King_James)/Acts#10:10 "s:Bible (King James)/Acts")). In the vision, Simon Peter sees all manner of beasts and fowl being lowered from [Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaven "Heaven") in a sheet. A voice commands Simon Peter to eat. When he objects to eating those animals that are [unclean according to Mosaic Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashrut "Kashrut"), the voice tells him not to call unclean that which God has cleansed.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-oca-7)

When Cornelius' men arrive, Simon Peter understands that through this vision the Lord had commanded him to preach the Word of God to the Gentiles. Peter accompanies Cornelius' men back to Caesarea.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-oca-7) When Cornelius meets Simon Peter, he falls at Peter's feet. Simon Peter raises the centurion, and the two men share their visions. Simon Peter tells of [Jesus' ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Jesus "Ministry of Jesus") and the [Resurrection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resurrection_of_Jesus "Resurrection of Jesus"); the [Holy Spirit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Spirit "Holy Spirit") descends on everyone at the gathering. The [Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jew "Jew") among the group are amazed that Cornelius and other [uncircumcised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumcision_controversy_in_early_Christianity "Circumcision controversy in early Christianity") should begin [speaking in tongues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaking_in_tongues "Speaking in tongues"), praising God. Thereupon Simon Peter commands that Cornelius and his followers, "kinsmen and near friends", be [baptized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptism "Baptism").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-cocn-8) The controversial aspect of Gentile conversion is taken up later at the [Council of Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Jerusalem "Council of Jerusalem") ([Acts 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_15 "Acts 15")).

### Religious situation of Judea

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cornelius_the_Centurion&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Religious situation of Judea")]

Taking into account that Judea had been within the Hellenic orbit since the conquest of [Alexander the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_the_Great "Alexander the Great"), there was time for wise men and philosophers, both Greek and Jewish, to exchange knowledge, thus beginning the syncretism between [Hellenism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenistic_religion "Hellenistic religion") and [Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaism "Judaism"), a phenomenon that occurred in the rest of his empire. Later with the arrival of the [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") (already Hellenized), there were no problems of [religious tolerance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_tolerance "Religious tolerance") (except in the case of the [Zealots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealots "Zealots")), since thanks to the _[interpretatio graeca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpretatio\_graeca "Interpretatio graeca")_ exported by the [Macedonians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonia_(ancient_kingdom) "Macedonia (ancient kingdom)"), it was possible to identify [Caelus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caelus "Caelus") (Roman god) or [Uranus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uranus_(mythology) "Uranus (mythology)") (his Greek equivalent) and [Yahweh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahweh "Yahweh") as the Supreme [God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God "God"), allowing conversion cases like Cornelius.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-11)

Significance
------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cornelius_the_Centurion&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Significance")]

[![Image 14: An angel appears before a man in armor kneeling in prayer](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d6/Gerbrand_van_den_Eeckhout_-_Vision_of_Cornelius_the_Centurion_-_Walters_372492.jpg/250px-Gerbrand_van_den_Eeckhout_-_Vision_of_Cornelius_the_Centurion_-_Walters_372492.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gerbrand_van_den_Eeckhout_-_Vision_of_Cornelius_the_Centurion_-_Walters_372492.jpg)

In this painting by [Gerbrand van den Eeckhout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerbrand_van_den_Eeckhout "Gerbrand van den Eeckhout") an angel appears to the Roman centurion Cornelius. The angel tells him to seek out St. Peter.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-12) The Walters Art Museum.

> Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, which have received the Holy Ghost as well as we?

— Acts 10:47

Cornelius is considered to be one of the first gentile converts to Christianity.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-13) The baptism of Cornelius is an important event in the history of the early Christian church, along with the conversion and baptism of the [Ethiopian eunuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_eunuch "Ethiopian eunuch"). The Christian church was first formed around the original disciples and followers of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus "Jesus"), all of whom—including Jesus—were [Galilean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilean "Galilean"), except for [Judas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judas_Iscariot "Judas Iscariot") who was Judean. Males in the Judean community were Jews: they were circumcised and observed the [Law of Moses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/613_commandments "613 commandments"). The reception of Cornelius sparked a debate among the leaders of the new community of followers of Jesus, culminating in the decision to allow Gentiles to become Christians without conforming to Jewish requirements for circumcision, as recounted in [Acts 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_15 "Acts 15").

Legacy
------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cornelius_the_Centurion&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Legacy")]

His feast day on the new [Martyrologium Romanum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martyrologium_Romanum "Martyrologium Romanum") is 20 October. He is commemorated in the Orthodox tradition on 13 September.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-oca-7) Cornelius is honored on the [liturgical calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calendar_of_saints_(Episcopal_Church) "Calendar of saints (Episcopal Church)") of the [Episcopal Church in the United States of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(United_States) "Episcopal Church (United States)") on [February 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_4 "February 4").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-teccalendar-2) The [Armenian Apostolic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_Apostolic_Church "Armenian Apostolic Church") commemorates Cornelius on the Tuesday after the third Sunday of [Advent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advent "Advent").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-14)

Certain traditions hold Cornelius as becoming either the first [bishop of Caesarea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Caesarea "Bishop of Caesarea"), or the bishop of [Scepsis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scepsis "Scepsis") in [Mysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysia "Mysia").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-cathen-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-cocn-8) The Greek-French philosopher [Cornelius Castoriadis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_Castoriadis "Cornelius Castoriadis") was named after him.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-15) When [Governors Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governors_Island "Governors Island") in New York City was a military installation, the Episcopal Church maintained a [stone chapel there dedicated to him](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion "Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-16)

The **Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion** is an [Episcopal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(United_States) "Episcopal Church (United States)") chapel on [Governors Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governors_Island "Governors Island") in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), United States. It is part of the [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parish "Parish") of [Trinity Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Church_(Manhattan) "Trinity Church (Manhattan)") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan") and is dedicated in honor of [Cornelius the Centurion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_the_Centurion "Cornelius the Centurion"). The first building to bear this name was erected in 1847 thanks to the efforts of John McVickar, who had been serving as a chaplain at [Fort Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Jay "Fort Jay") on Governors Island since 1844.[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-fort_name-2) By the beginning of the 20th century, this building was condemned and replaced by the current building, which was designed by architect [Charles C. Haight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_C._Haight "Charles C. Haight") and dedicated in 1906. The building was constructed in the [English Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Gothic_architecture "English Gothic architecture") and [Gothic Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_Revival_architecture "Gothic Revival architecture") architectural styles.

For various periods in its history, chaplains have been provided from different sources, including from Trinity Church, the Army's chaplain services, and the [United States Navy Chaplain Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_Chaplain_Corps "United States Navy Chaplain Corps"). Since the closure of the military outpost on Governors Island in 1996, the building has been under the sole ownership of Trinity Church. In the 21st century, the building has served as a venue for performing arts and art installations. As of 2014, it did not hold religious services.
