Reverend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Reverend "The Reverend") John McVickar, a professor at [Columbia College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_College,_Columbia_University "Columbia College, Columbia University") and [Episcopalian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(United_States) "Episcopal Church (United States)") priest, accepted an offer to serve as a [chaplain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaplain "Chaplain") at [Fort Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Jay "Fort Jay") on [Governors Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governors_Island "Governors Island").[[note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-fort_name-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973155-4) McVickar initially held religious services in an office building, but in 1847, with support from [Major General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_general_(United_States) "Major general (United States)")[Winfield Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winfield_Scott "Winfield Scott"), he formulated plans for a dedicated [chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel "Chapel") building at the fort.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973155-4) He did not receive government funding for the building, but was able to raise money via donations from churchgoers in Manhattan.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973155-4) McVickar also donated a significant amount of his own money towards the building's erection.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973155-4) The building, designed by McVickar,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChorley194769-3) was dedicated as the Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion by Bishop [William H. DeLancey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_H._DeLancey "William H. DeLancey") of the [Episcopal Diocese of Western New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Diocese_of_Western_New_York "Episcopal Diocese of Western New York") on April 19, 1847.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973156-5) The construction cost several thousand dollars.[[note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-8)

In 1850, McVickar's services expanded to include [Bedloe's Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Island "Liberty Island"), where the Army had relocated some of the recruiting services.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDix195079-6) In 1862, following the outbreak of the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") reworked its policy regarding chaplains, requiring civilian chaplains to reside permanently on their bases.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973156-5) Since McVickar was unable to reside permanently on the island, he resigned, with the Army stationing one of their own chaplains at the fort.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973156-5) He was initially succeeded by a man named Scudder,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith1923185-9) a minister of the [Dutch Reformed Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Reformed_Church "Dutch Reformed Church"), who retired in 1865.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDix195079-6) Scudder was replaced by James Armout Moore La Tourette of the Episcopal Church, who served until 1868.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDix195079-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith1923185-9)

### Parish of Trinity Church

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Parish of Trinity Church")]

[![Image 4: A gathering of people outside the St. Anne's Chapel at Fort Missoula](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion%2C_c._1900.jpg/250px-Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion%2C_c._1900.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion,_c._1900.jpg)

The original chapel building, c. 1900

The Army provided a military chaplain for the chapel for the duration of the war, but in 1868, they discontinued this program, stating that ministerial services should be provided by a local church elsewhere in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973156-5) That year, the [clergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clergy "Clergy") of [Trinity Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Church_(Manhattan) "Trinity Church (Manhattan)"), geographically one of the closest churches to the chapel, entered into an agreement with the [United States Department of War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_War "United States Department of War") wherein the church would maintain a chaplain on the island if the government provided housing and other necessities that they would normally provide to military chaplains.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973156-5) Additionally, Trinity Church would receive free use of the chapel building for their religious services.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973156-5) In a 1973 book on the [parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parish "Parish")'s history, Episcopalian journalist [Clifford Phelps Morehouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Phelps_Morehouse "Clifford Phelps Morehouse") stated that the arrangement, which was formally agreed upon in August,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith1923186-10)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDix195080-11) was "unique among army posts".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973156-5) St. Cornelius was one of a number of chapels added to the parish in the late 1860s, alongside [St. Augustine's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Augustine%27s_Church_(Manhattan) "St. Augustine's Church (Manhattan)") and St. Chrysostom's.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973154%E2%80%93155-12)

### Current chapel building

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Current chapel building")]

In the early 20th century, the chapel building was [condemned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condemned_property "Condemned property"), prompting the creation of a replacement building.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1986-13) Architect [Charles C. Haight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_C._Haight "Charles C. Haight") designed this new building.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDolkartPostal2004366-14) The [cornerstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornerstone "Cornerstone") was laid on October 27, 1905, by [Coadjutor Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coadjutor_Bishop "Coadjutor Bishop")[David H. Greer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_H._Greer "David H. Greer") of the [Episcopal Diocese of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Diocese_of_New_York "Episcopal Diocese of New York").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChorley194772-15) Coincidentally, Haight's father, [Benjamin I. Haight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_I._Haight "Benjamin I. Haight"), had previously served as an assistant minister at Trinity Church.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChorley194771%E2%80%9372-16) Work was completed in 1906.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973156-5) On October 19 of that year,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDix1950257-17) the building was consecrated by Bishop Greer in a ceremony attended by both clergy of Trinity Church and military officials.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973210-18) Greer substituted for Bishop [Henry C. Potter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_C._Potter "Henry C. Potter"), who was unable to preside over the consecration due to a recent death in his family.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDix1950258-19) The sermon for the event was written by [Morgan Dix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Dix "Morgan Dix"), Trinity Church's [rector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rector_(ecclesiastical) "Rector (ecclesiastical)"), and read by assistant rector [William T. Manning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_T._Manning "William T. Manning").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973210-18)

In November 1910, a military memorial service honoring American soldiers was held at the chapel, with several notable New Yorkers and members of the military in attendance.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1910-20) Current military officers included Major General [Frederick Dent Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Dent_Grant "Frederick Dent Grant") of the [Department of the East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_the_East "Department of the East"), and [Lieutenant Colonels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_colonel_(United_States) "Lieutenant colonel (United States)")[Adelbert Cronkhite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelbert_Cronkhite "Adelbert Cronkhite"), [John A. Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Hull "John A. Hull"), and [Isaac Littell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Littell "Isaac Littell"), while retired military members included [Asa Bird Gardiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asa_Bird_Gardiner "Asa Bird Gardiner"), [John White Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_White_Moore "John White Moore"), [Charles Augustus Schermerhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Augustus_Schermerhorn "Charles Augustus Schermerhorn"), and [Andrew C. Zabriskie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_C._Zabriskie "Andrew C. Zabriskie").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1910-20)

#### Military flags and trophies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Military flags and trophies")]

Following the dedication, the chapel's [vicar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicar "Vicar"), Edmund Banks Smith, began a project to beautify the building by adding [military flags](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_colours,_standards_and_guidons "Military colours, standards and guidons") and other decorations.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973210-18) In 1907, the church accepted five flags from the [1st Regiment of New York Volunteers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Regiment_of_New_York_Volunteers "1st Regiment of New York Volunteers") that had been carried during the [Mexican–American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War "Mexican–American War").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1907-21) They were presented to the chapel by five veterans of that regiment in a large ceremony attended by representatives of various military and civic organizations, including the [Society of the Cincinnati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_the_Cincinnati "Society of the Cincinnati"), the [General Society of the War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Society_of_the_War_of_1812 "General Society of the War of 1812"), the [Aztec Club of 1847](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztec_Club_of_1847 "Aztec Club of 1847"), and the [Military Order of the Loyal Legion of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Order_of_the_Loyal_Legion_of_the_United_States "Military Order of the Loyal Legion of the United States").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1907-21) Notable individuals present, either in a military capacity or as representatives of the organizations, included Major General Grant, [Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiral_(United_States) "Admiral (United States)")[Caspar F. Goodrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspar_F._Goodrich "Caspar F. Goodrich"), [F. Burrall Hoffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._Burrall_Hoffman "F. Burrall Hoffman"), [Francis Key Pendleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Key_Pendleton "Francis Key Pendleton"), [Herbert L. Satterlee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_L._Satterlee "Herbert L. Satterlee"), and [Cornelius Vanderbilt III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_Vanderbilt_III "Cornelius Vanderbilt III").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1907-21)

In 1915, _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ published an article discussing the flags kept at the chapel, which by that time numbered over fifty.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1915-22) Most of the larger flags were hung from the rafters in the [nave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nave "Nave"), while flags from the Mexican–American War were hung in the south [transept](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transept "Transept") and the [cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalry "Cavalry")[guidons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guidon_(United_States) "Guidon (United States)") were displayed in the [choir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choir_(architecture) "Choir (architecture)").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1915-22) At the time, the oldest flag dated back to approximately 1787, while the most recent was a large American flag from the [Boxer Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxer_Rebellion "Boxer Rebellion").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1915-22) In 1921, the [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army") donated a regimental color from the [King's Royal Rifle Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Royal_Rifle_Corps "King's Royal Rifle Corps") to the chapel as a gesture of goodwill between the United Kingdom and the United States.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1921-23) By 2010, the chapel housed 87 battle flags.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhiteWillenskyLeadon2010951-24)

In 1924, Smith retired.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973249-25) Subsequently, the Army and Trinity Church came to a new agreement regarding the chapel's vicars.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973249%E2%80%93250-26)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1986-13) The Army would provide a military chaplain for the chapel who would be a priest in the Episcopal Church and would subsequently be made an honorary vicar of Trinity Church.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973156-5) This arrangement existed for the duration of the Army's presence on the island.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973250-27) In 1955, the first man was commissioned into the [United States Army Nurse Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Nurse_Corps "United States Army Nurse Corps") in a ceremony at the chapel.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1955-28)

On December 31, 1965, the Army closed its fort on Governors Island; the [United States Coast Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Coast_Guard "United States Coast Guard") planned to use the facility starting the following June.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973293%E2%80%93294-29) Around that time, a historical plaque was erected outside the chapel.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973293%E2%80%93294-29) In the interim, the current Army vicar remained at the post until the Coast Guard took over.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973293%E2%80%93294-29) Chaplains were subsequently supplied by the [United States Navy Chaplain Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy_Chaplain_Corps "United States Navy Chaplain Corps"),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrinityChurchNYC.org2014-30) with the same agreement in place with Trinity that resulted in these chaplains being named honorary vicars.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorehouse1973312%E2%80%93313-31)

Starting in the 1970s, Trinity Church began to face financial difficulties that affected its administration of the chapel.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1986-13) In 1976, Trinity Church paid for a new lighting system for the chapel, but this would be the last major investment in the building for a decade.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1986-13) Following this, the building went into a state of disrepair, needing roof repairs and improvements to its pipe organ system.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1986-13) According to _The New York Times_, Trinity Church found it difficult to finance repairs because the building was located on government property, while the government was unable to help with repairs due to regulations regarding privately owned structures.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1986-13) In 1980, the church began to lease the chapel to the government for $1 (equivalent to $3.82 in 2024) per year.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrinityChurchNYC.org2014-30)

In March 1986, Trinity Church agreed to turn over ownership of the building to the government, with a provision that the church would regain ownership if the building were not used for religious purposes.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1986-13) According to The Reverend Norman L. Cram Jr., the chaplain, "It's a necessary move, because the government has to own the chapel in order to put money into it. And the building really ought to be maintained by the government since it is used exclusively by government employees."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1986-13) At the time, the building was valued at approximately $3 million ($8.6 million in 2024).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1986-13) The move was also part of a larger series of divestitures by Trinity Church going back to the 1970s, when the church began to suffer financially.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1986-13) By the end of the year, the only chapel under Trinity's purview would be [St. Paul's Chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Paul%27s_Chapel "St. Paul's Chapel").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1986-13)

### Fort closure and recent history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Fort closure and recent history")]

[![Image 5: Church interior featuring a wooden floor, white walls, arched windows, and a glimpse of the altar at the far end](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/St_Cornelius_Chapel%2C_Governors_Island_1.jpg/250px-St_Cornelius_Chapel%2C_Governors_Island_1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:St_Cornelius_Chapel,_Governors_Island_1.jpg)

The chapel _(interior pictured 2012)_ has hosted numerous public events in the 21st century, including several art installations.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVogel2009-32)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTESierzputowski2018-33)

In 1996, the [New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Landmarks_Preservation_Commission "New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission") declared the part of the island that included the chapel as the Governors Island [Historic District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historic_District "Historic District").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDolkartPostal2004366-14) That same year, the Coast Guard ceased use of the island and, as a result, the chapel came back under the ownership of Trinity Church.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrinityChurchNYC.org2014-30)

In 2005, the island opened to the public as a [park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park "Park").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWalsh2011-34) Since then, the chapel has been used for a number of public events. In 2008, the chapel held screenings as part of that year's [African Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Film_Festival,_Inc. "African Film Festival, Inc.").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraeber2008-35) A year later, the [nonprofit group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_organization "Nonprofit organization")[Creative Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Time "Creative Time") held an expansive free [art exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_exhibition "Art exhibition") on the island.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVogel2009-32)[Anthony McCall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_McCall "Anthony McCall") installed a [light art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_art "Light art") piece inside the chapel and Klaus Weber displayed a [wind chime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_chime "Wind chime") outside the building.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2009-36)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKilgannon2009-37) In 2014, the [Reggie Wilson/Fist and Heel Performance Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Wilson/Fist_and_Heel_Performance_Group "Reggie Wilson/Fist and Heel Performance Group") held a stage production at the chapel.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKourlas2014-38) By that year, the chapel was only one of two in the parish of Trinity Church, though it was not in active use.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTETrinityChurchNYC.org2014-30)[Gia Kourlas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gia_Kourlas "Gia Kourlas") of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ described the building at that time as having "crumbling white walls".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKourlas2014-38) In 2018, the chapel was host to "The Eclipse",[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDermon2018-39) an art installation by [Jacob Hashimoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Hashimoto "Jacob Hashimoto") that consisted of thousands of paper kites displayed throughout the building.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBoyer-DryRao2018-40)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTESierzputowski2018-33)

The chapel in 2008

The chapel's architectural style has been described as both [English Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Gothic_architecture "English Gothic architecture")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1986-13) and [Gothic Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_Revival_architecture "Gothic Revival architecture").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDolkartPostal2004366-14)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhiteWillenskyLeadon2010951-24) The exterior is clad in [coursed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Course_(architecture) "Course (architecture)") and [rusticated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rustication_(architecture) "Rustication (architecture)") limestone.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansenPearson19964,_15-41) The overall shape of the building is generally [cruciform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruciform#Cruciform_architectural_plan "Cruciform"), and it has length and width measurements of approximately 106 feet (32 m) by 70 ft (21 m).[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansenPearson199673-42) The northwest corner has a three-story square tower containing the main entrance at ground level, while a four-[turret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turret_(architecture) "Turret (architecture)")[parapet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parapet "Parapet") caps it.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansenPearson199673-42) The roof is made of [slate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate "Slate") and features [copper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper "Copper") finishings, including [rain gutters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_gutter "Rain gutter").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansenPearson199673-42) There are 35 [stained glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stained_glass "Stained glass") windows, many of which are [lancet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancet_window "Lancet window")-shaped.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansenPearson199673-42) On the east side of the building is the cornerstone, which bears the inscription "A.D. 1905".[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHansenPearson199673-42)

The interior of the building consists of white walls and houses a [pipe organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pipe_organ "Pipe organ").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTE''The_New_York_Times''1986-13) Additionally, there are three [sedilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedilia "Sedilia") located in the [sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctuary#Sanctuary_as_area_around_the_altar "Sanctuary").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDix195079-6) Of these, the main one is dedicated to McVickar,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDix195079-6) and the other two are dedicated to fellow vicars Davidson and La Tourette.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDix195082-43) McVickar's sedilia bears the following inscription:[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith1923185-9)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChorley194770-44)

> In / Memory of / John McVickar / Priest and Doctor / Born 1787, Died 1868 / Chaplain of this Post / 1844–1862 / By whose wisdom and / liberality the first / Chapel of St. Cornelius / the Centurion was / erected in 1846 / The law of truth / was in his mouth, / and iniquity / was not found in / his lips.

La Tourette's sedilia says the following:[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith1923186-10)

> In / Memory of / James Armour Moore / La Tourette / Priest. / Born 1826. Died 1891. / Chaplain of this / Post, / 1865–1868. / Faithful in the dis- / charge of duty, notably / in the siege of Asiatic / cholera of 1866. / Instant in season / Out of season.

Finally, Davidson's bears the following inscription:[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChorley194771-45)

> In Memory of the Rev. / Alexander Davidson / Chaplain at Fort Columbus / New York Harbor / Who died of Yellow Fever / Sept. A. D. 1870. / Though absent on sick leave when the disease broke out he came back, and while ministering to the sick and dying, was himself struck down and thus gave his life for his Brethren.

The chapel is located near the intersection of Barry Road and Evans Road,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhiteWillenskyLeadon2010951-24) at the west end of Nolan Park.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWalsh2010-46)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Cornelius_the_Centurion#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWalsh2011-34)

St. Cornelius the Centurion
===========================

 February 5, 2014 

News and Notes

_February 7 is the feast day of Cornelius the Centurion in the Episcopal calendar. In honor of his feast, here's a little background on the Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion, one of the two remaining chapels of Trinity Parish._

![Image 25: Original St. Cornelius Chapel](https://trinitychurchnyc.org/sites/default/files/styles/content_width_100/public/2021-05/OriginalStCornelius.jpg?itok=4suZxlAc)

 From the Archives of Trinity Church Wall Street 

_The original Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion_

The Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion was built on Governors Island, a military outpost in New York Harbor, in 1846 through the efforts of the army chaplain, the Rev. John McVickar. Trinity Church provided McVickar and his successors with continuous support. By 1866, the War Department stopped providing chaplains to Governor’s Island. Trinity Church offered to maintain a chaplain at her own cost if the army would agree to place the chapel under the parish’s control. St. Cornelius became a part of Trinity Parish as a free chapel in 1868.

![Image 26: Consecration of the 2nd St. Cornelius Chapel](https://trinitychurchnyc.org/sites/default/files/styles/content_width_100/public/2021-05/ConsecrationStCornelius.jpg?itok=Z5u3lmDX)

 From the Archives of Trinity Church Wall Street 

_The consecration of the second Chapel of St. Cornelius the Centurion_

The Parish replaced the small wooden church with a new chapel designed by Charles C. Haight in 1906. In 1924, the agreement between the Army and Trinity was modified so that the Army paid the chaplain’s salary while Trinity maintained the building. St. Cornelius’ chaplains were honorary vicars and part of parish clergy. A 1954 agreement allowed chaplains from other Protestant denominations to use St. Cornelius to conduct services. This arrangement lasted until 1966, when the army turned over control of Governor’s Island to the U.S. Coast Guard. Under the Coast Guard, the Navy Chaplain Corps had the responsibility of assigning chaplains.

In the early 1970s, Trinity parish discontinued ordinary maintenance and janitorial services for St. Cornelius, but it continued to assist with major maintenance and provide insurance coverage

In 1980, the parish and St. Cornelius reached an agreement by which Trinity would lease the chapel to the U.S. Government for $1 per year. Then in 1986, Trinity donated the chapel to the U.S. Government, under the stipulation that it would revert to the parish if the government ceased to own the land underlying the chapel or to use the building as a military chapel. The Coast Guard vacated Governor’s Island in 1996, and Trinity regained ownership of the chapel, which is no longer in use.

![Image 27: Flags at St. Cornelius](https://trinitychurchnyc.org/sites/default/files/styles/content_width_100/public/2021-05/FlagsStCornelius.jpg?itok=6O3jvRkM)

 From the Archives of Trinity Church Wall Street 

_In the 1920s, flags displayed at St. Cornelius were restored. We loved this photo and are researching the flags and the restoration process. We'll report back soon!_
